links.note: 711 tells those who know the body of words (சொல்லின் தொகையறிந்த) to speak after knowing the assembly (அவையறிந்து ஆராய்ந்து சொல்லுக). 644 gives the same command in the chapter on eloquence, திறனறிந்து சொல்லுக, which Parimelazhagar takes as knowing one's own and the hearers' capacities, and adds that no virtue or gain exceeds it. The pair shows the audience rule stated once as a rule of speech and once as a rule of the court.

Both verses end with the identical line சொல்லின் தொகையறிந்த தூய்மையவர். 711 commands such people to know the assembly before speaking; 721 says that, having known the kinds (வகையறிந்து), they do not let their speech slip before the capable (வல்லவை வாய்சோரார்). The repeated line makes 721 the outcome of 711's instruction: knowing the assembly is what removes the fear that causes slips.

712 asks the speaker in an assembly to discern the opening (இடைதெரிந்து), which Parimelazhagar glosses as the hearers' readiness to listen. 696 asks the same of one speaking to a king: know his mood and consider the time (குறிப்பறிந்து காலங் கருதி) and say it so that it is wanted. The timing rule is the same before an assembly and before a single ruler.

712 says to discern the opening and understand clearly before speaking (இடைதெரிந்து நன்குணர்ந்து சொல்லுக). 687 ranks highest the envoy who considers the time, knows the place and speaks after thinking it through (காலங் கருதி இடனறிந்து எண்ணி உரைப்பான்). Both make the moment, not only the content, part of speaking well; Parimelazhagar glosses both with the same word, செவ்வி.

713 says those who take up speaking without knowing the assembly (அவையறியார்) do not know the kinds of speech and have no ability at all. 401 says holding forth in an assembly (கோட்டி கொளல்) without full learning is like playing dice with no marked board. Each names a different missing precondition for speaking in an assembly, knowledge of the hearers in 713 and knowledge of the books in 401, and each treats the speech that results as empty.

714 uses a colour pair for intelligence: be bright (ஒள்ளியர்) before the bright, and take the colour of white plaster (வான்சுதை வண்ணம்) before the blank (வெளியார்). 844 uses the same pair: whiteness (வெண்மை) is the conceit that says 'we have brightness' (ஒண்மை உடையம் யாம்). Read together, the learned person of 714 puts on whiteness knowingly before those who, by 844, are white because they think themselves bright.

714 tells the speaker to change with the audience, bright before the bright and blank before the blank. 425 says understanding is what does not open and close (மலர்தலும் கூம்பலும் இல்லது அறிவு). If 425's second half is read generally, as steadiness of bearing, the two disagree about whether the wise adapt their display; on Parimelazhagar's reading, where 425 is about constancy in friendship with the world, the conflict disappears.

715 calls the restraint of not speaking first among elders (முதுவருள் முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு) the best of good things. 403 says even the unlearned are very good if they can stay silent before the learned (கற்றார்முன் சொல்லாதிருக்கப் பெறின்). 403 asks silence of those with nothing to say; 715 asks those who do have something to say only to hold back from going first, which Parimelazhagar notes still allows speaking with or after the elders.

715 praises the restraint (செறிவு) of not speaking first among elders. 419 says a mouth that bows (வணங்கிய வாய்) is hard to have for those without fine listening. Both treat modest speech as a mark of what a person has learned, and 419 supplies the source 715 leaves unstated: the habit of listening.

716 says a slip (இழுக்கு) before those who have taken in wide learning is like faltering from one's footing on the path. 957 says a fault in the well-born shows up high, like the spot on the moon (மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல்). In both, the weight of a fault depends on where it is seen, the standing of the witnesses in 716 and of the person in 957, and not only on its size.

642 gives the general rule: since gain and ruin come from speech, guard against a lapse in it (சொல்லின்கட் சோர்வு). 716 applies it to one setting, a slip before the widely learned, and measures the damage by comparing it to falling from the path (ஆற்றின் நிலைதளர்ந்தற்று), which Parimelazhagar reads as a renouncer's lapse from the good path.

717 says the learning of those who have studied and understood shines among those able to examine words without fault (சொல்தெரிதல் வல்லார் அகத்து). 404 says the wise do not accept an unlearned person's brightness (ஒட்பம்), however good it is. The same expert hearers decide both cases: before them real learning becomes visible and untaught cleverness is not accepted.

718 compares speaking before people of understanding to pouring water on a bed where the crop is already growing (பாத்தியுள் நீர் சொரிந்தற்று). In 1093 the man says her glance and lowered head were water poured on the growing bond between them (யாப்பினுள் அட்டிய நீர்). Both use irrigation for a response that makes something already alive grow, learning in one and love in the other; 1093 is a lover's speech, not a teaching.

718 and 720 are the chapter's two liquid images. Words before those who understand are water poured on a growing bed; words before those not of one's own kind are nectar spilled in a dirty yard (அங்கணத்துள் உக்க அமிழ்து). The second limits the first: the worth of what is poured does not save it, and nectar, which is worth more than water, is lost where water in the right bed is not.

719 and 728 share the phrase நல்லவையுள் நன்கு செலச் சொல்லு-. 728 says those who cannot speak tellingly in a good assembly are of no use though they have learned much; 719 tells those who can do so not to speak in a mean assembly even by forgetting (பொச்சாந்தும் சொல்லற்க). Together they set the limits: silence in a good assembly is a failure, and silence in a mean one is required.

719 forbids speaking good things in a mean assembly. 849 gives a reason in another chapter: one who shows something to a person who does not see becomes himself unseeing (காணாதான் காட்டுவான் தான்காணான்), while that person goes on seeing as he saw. Parimelazhagar makes the same point on 719, that both assemblies would then look down on the speaker.

720 says holding forth before those not of one's kind is like nectar spilled in a dirty yard (அங்கணத்துள் உக்க அமிழ்து). 1000 says great wealth in the hands of one without courtesy is like good milk spoiled by the fault of its vessel (கலந்தீமையால் திரிந்தற்று). Both describe a fine liquid ruined by where it lands, and so place the loss in the receiver and not in the thing given.

720 and 401 both use the phrase கோட்டி கொளல், holding forth in a gathering. 401 condemns it when the speaker lacks full learning (நிரம்பிய நூலின்றி); 720 condemns it when the hearers are not of the speaker's kind (தங்கணத்தார் அல்லார்முன்). The two verses cover the two ways the same act fails, from the speaker's side and from the audience's.

721 says those who know the body of words and the kinds of assembly do not let their speech slip before the capable (வாய்சோரார்), which Parimelazhagar reads as not slipping out of fear. 647 lists the same qualities, able to speak, without slips, without fear (சொலல்வல்லன் சோர்விலன் அஞ்சான்), and says such a person is hard for anyone to defeat. 647 states the payoff of the fearlessness that 721 describes.

716 says a slip (இழுக்கு) before those of wide learning is like falling from the path. 721 answers from the next chapter: those who know words and know the assembly do not slip before the capable (வல்லவை வாய்சோரார்). One verse gives the cost of the slip and the other says what prevents it.

722 says those who make what they have learned go home before the learned (கற்ற செலச் சொல்லுவார்) are called learned among the learned. 424 defines understanding with the same verb: saying things so that they go in easily (எண்பொருளவாகச் செலச்சொல்லி) and seeing the subtle meaning in what others say. Both measure learning or understanding by whether it reaches the hearer, not by what the speaker holds.

722 gives the title 'learned among the learned' to those who can convey their learning to the learned. 650 gives the reverse case: those who cannot unfold what they have learned so that others understand (கற்றது உணர விரித்துரையாதார்) are like flowers that bloom in clusters without scent. Together they treat communication as part of learning itself.

723 says those who will die amid enemies are easy to find, and those who do not fear within an assembly are hard to find (அவையகத்து அஞ்சாதவர்). 872 says one may take on the enmity of those who plough with the bow but not of those who plough with the word (சொல்லேர் உழவர்). Both rank the word above the weapon, 723 by how rare the courage is and 872 by how dangerous the opponent is.

723 calls those who die amid enemies எளியர், easy to find. 762 says the hardness that does not fear wounds when the king falters is rare except in an old army (தொல்படைக்கல்லால் அரிது). If 723's first half is read as saying battle courage is common, the two disagree about how rare it is; if 762 is limited to courage in defeat and with reduced numbers, they do not.

724 says to make what you have learned go home before the learned and to take what is more from those who know more (மிக்காருள் மிக்க கொளல்). 646 says the way of the spotless is to speak so that others want it and to take the benefit of what others say (பிறர்சொல் பயன்கோடல்). Both describe speaking in company as an exchange in which the speaker also learns.

724 joins two acts: convey your learning (செலச்சொல்லி) and take in what those more learned have. 424 joins the same two as its definition of understanding: say things so that they go in (செலச்சொல்லி) and see the subtle meaning in what others say (பிறர்வாய் நுண்பொருள் காண்பது). What 424 calls understanding, 724 presents as what a fearless speaker gains from an assembly.

725 says to learn by the proper path and with measure (ஆற்றின் அளவறிந்து கற்க) in order to reply in the assembly without fear; Parimelazhagar takes அளவு as the science of logic. 645 says to speak a word only after knowing no other word can defeat it (வெல்லுஞ்சொல் இன்மை அறிந்து). 725 names the training that makes 645's test possible.

Both verses open with the command to learn. 391 says learn without flaw and then stand in keeping with it (கற்க கசடற ... நிற்க அதற்குத் தக); 725 says learn with measure so as to give a fearless reply (மாற்றங் கொடுத்தற் பொருட்டு). 391 gives learning its end in conduct, and 725 gives it a second end in public speech.

726 asks what a sword is to those who are not hard-eyed, and what books are to those who fear a subtle assembly (நுண்ணவை அஞ்சுபவர்க்கு). 534 says the fearful have no fortress (அச்சமுடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை), which Parimelazhagar explains as a fortress being of no use to them. In each, fear cancels an instrument that is sound in itself: sword, books, fort.

726 says books are nothing to one who fears a subtle assembly. 647 says the one who can speak, does not slip and does not fear (அஞ்சான்) is hard for anyone to defeat, and Parimelazhagar takes that fearlessness as fearlessness of the assembly. 647 states positively the condition whose absence 726 says makes learning useless.

727 says the book learned by one who fears the assembly is a bright sword in the hand of a பேடி among enemies (பேடிகை ஒள்வாள்). 614 uses the same figure for another failing: the generosity of one without effort comes to nothing like a sword in the hand of a பேடி (பேடிகை வாளாண்மை). The shared figure puts unused learning and unbacked generosity under one pattern, a good instrument held by someone who will not use it.

728 says those who cannot speak tellingly in a good assembly are of no use (பயமிலரே) though they have learned many things. 650 says those who cannot unfold what they have learned so that others understand are like clustered flowers without scent (நாறா மலரனையர்). The two verses make the same claim, one in plain terms in the chapter on fear of the assembly and one by image in the chapter on eloquence.

728 and 140 have the same form: 'though they have learned much'. In 140, those who have not learned to live in accord with the world are without understanding though they have learned much (பலகற்றும்). In 728, those who cannot speak well in a good assembly are without use though they have learned many things (பல்லவை கற்றும்). Each names a practical ability without which the amount learned does not count.

395 calls the unlearned the lowest (கடையரே கல்லாதவர்). 729 uses the same word to put someone beneath them: those who have studied and understood and still fear an assembly of the good are lower than the unlearned (கல்லாதவரின் கடை). 729 thus limits 395's ranking, since learning that is not voiced does not lift a person above the bottom rank and, as Parimelazhagar explains, leaves them with only the labour of having studied.

403 says the unlearned are very good if they stay silent before the learned (கற்றார்முன் சொல்லாதிருக்கப் பெறின்). 729 says the learned who fear a good assembly are lower than the unlearned. The same silence before the same kind of audience is credited to one person and held against the other, so its value depends on whether the silent person has something to give.

730 says those who fear the arena and cannot convey what they have learned are like those who are not, though they exist (உளரெனினும் இல்லாரொடு ஒப்பர்). 406 says the unlearned can only be said to exist (உளரென்னும் மாத்திரையர்) and are otherwise like barren salt land. The shared figure of bare existence puts the silent learned in the same place as the unlearned, which is the conclusion 729 states directly.

730 counts those who cannot voice their learning as equal to those who are not, though they exist. 214 says one who knows what is fitting truly lives and anyone else is placed among the dead (செத்தாருள் வைக்கப்படும்). Both apply the figure of a living person counted as dead or absent to someone who gives nothing to others, wealth in 214 and learning in 730; Parimelazhagar reads 730's இல்லார் as the dead.
